_about: answer = index of the right option (shuffled on screen); evidence = supporting sentence, review only; hint = gentle "look again" line.

man-who-died.q: What game did Scudder and Hannay play every night?
man-who-died.evidence: He read and smoked a bit, and made a heap of jottings in a notebook, and every night we had a game of chess, at which he beat me hollow.
man-who-died.hint: Think about the evenings in the flat.

man-who-died.q: Why was Scudder hiding in Hannay’s flat?
options: He had nowhere else to live
man-who-died.evidence: The gentry who are after me are pretty bright-eyed citizens.
man-who-died.hint: Think about what Scudder tells Hannay on the first night.

man-who-died.q: Scudder says, “I happen at this moment to be dead.” What does he mean?
options: He has tricked his enemies into thinking he is dead
man-who-died.evidence: You see, I happen at this moment to be dead.”
man-who-died.hint: Think about why someone hiding might want enemies to stop looking.

milkman.q: What did Hannay borrow from the milkman?
milkman.evidence: Lend me your cap and overall for ten minutes, and here’s a sovereign for you.”
milkman.hint: Think about how Hannay leaves the flat.

milkman.q: Why did Hannay wait in the hall early in the morning?
options: To meet the milkman and borrow his disguise
milkman.evidence: Then I hung about in the hall waiting for the milkman.
milkman.hint: Think about Hannay’s plan for getting out.

milkman.q: Hannay took fifty pounds in gold in a belt. Why was that wise?
options: He might have to stay on the run for a long time
He wanted to buy a car
milkman.evidence: I had drawn a good sum in gold from the bank two days before, in case Scudder should want money, and I took fifty pounds of it in sovereigns in a belt which I had brought back from Rhodesia.
milkman.hint: Think about what you need when you can’t go home.

innkeeper.q: What was Scudder’s notebook mostly filled with?
options: Figures, with a name printed now and then
innkeeper.evidence: It was pretty well filled with jottings, chiefly figures, though now and then a name was printed in.
innkeeper.hint: Think about when Hannay studies the notebook.

innkeeper.q: Who did Hannay think was in the monoplane over the moor?
options: A friend come to rescue him
innkeeper.evidence: I was as certain as if I had been told that that aeroplane was looking for me, and that it did not belong to the police.
innkeeper.hint: Think about the aeroplane in the sky.

innkeeper.q: Why did Hannay look for a key word to crack the cipher?
options: A key word gives the order of the letters in a number code
Every book has a key word
innkeeper.evidence: So I fastened on the printed words, for you can make a pretty good numerical cipher if you have a key word which gives you the sequence of the letters.
innkeeper.hint: Think about how number codes work.

candidate.q: What did the candidate hope Hannay was?
candidate.evidence: Are you by any blessed chance a Free Trader?”
candidate.hint: Think about the young man in the car.

candidate.q: Why did the candidate think Hannay could speak at his meeting?
options: He thought Hannay knew about the Colonies
candidate.evidence: You’re a Free Trader and can tell our people what a washout Protection is in the Colonies.
candidate.hint: Think about where Hannay had lived.

candidate.q: Hannay agrees to speak at a meeting he knows nothing about. What does that show about him?
options: He thinks fast and can play a part
He wanted to give himself up
candidate.evidence: Well, you see I’m Liberal Candidate for this part of the world, and I had a meeting on tonight at Brattleburn—that’s my chief town, and an infernal Tory stronghold.
candidate.hint: Think about how useful a disguise a speaker on a platform is.

roadman.q: Who did Hannay change places with on the moor road?
roadman.evidence: Then in a tiny bight of road, beside a heap of stones, I found the roadman.
roadman.hint: Think about the man beside the heap of stones.

roadman.q: Why did Hannay rub dust into his eyes?
options: A roadman’s eyes would look red and bleary
To hide them from the sun
roadman.evidence: A roadman’s eyes would no doubt be a little inflamed, so I contrived to get some dust in both of mine, and by dint of vigorous rubbing produced a bleary effect.
roadman.hint: Think about how carefully Hannay made his disguise.

roadman.q: Hannay borrowed the roadman’s spectacles, hat and even his old pipe. Why so many details?
options: A disguise works best when every small detail is right
roadman.evidence: I borrowed his spectacles and filthy old hat; stripped off coat, waistcoat, and collar, and gave him them to carry home; borrowed, too, the foul stump of a clay pipe as an extra property.
roadman.hint: Think about what the searchers might notice.

options: In a damp storeroom in the old farmhouse
archaeologist.evidence: The storeroom was a damp chamber in what had been the old farmhouse.
archaeologist.hint: Think about where Karl was told to put him.

archaeologist.q: Why was the storeroom so dark?
archaeologist.evidence: It was black as pitch, for the windows were heavily shuttered.

archaeologist.q: Once outside, how did Hannay get away without being seen?
options: He crawled from cover to cover up the hillside
archaeologist.evidence: I crawled out of my shelf into the cover of a boulder, and from it gained a shallow trench which slanted up the mountain face.
archaeologist.hint: Think about how he used the boulders and trenches.

fisherman.q: Who did Hannay decide he must reach in London?
options: Sir Walter Bullivant of the Foreign Office
fisherman.evidence: It seemed to me that the sooner I got in touch with the Foreign Office man, Sir Walter Bullivant, the better.
fisherman.hint: Think about who could help him.

fisherman.q: Why did the woman at the cottage give Hannay a plaid and an old hat?
options: She thought he was her husband
fisherman.evidence: At this I protested so strongly that I think she believed me honest, for she took the money and gave me a warm new plaid for it, and an old hat of her man’s.
fisherman.hint: Think about what made her trust him.

fisherman.q: Hannay thinks about telling a policeman the truth. Why is it so hard to be believed?
options: His true story sounds too strange to believe
fisherman.evidence: A policeman came up, and I should have told him the truth, and, if he didn’t believe it, demanded to be taken to Scotland Yard, or for that matter to the nearest police station.
fisherman.hint: Think about how wild Hannay’s story sounds.

vault.q: What did Scudder’s note say about the steps?
options: Thirty-nine steps — high tide at 10.17 p.m.
vault.evidence: Thirty-nine steps, I read, and again, thirty-nine steps—I counted them—high tide 10:17 p.m.
vault.hint: Think about the note they finally read.

vault.q: Why did they need a book of tide tables?
options: To find a place where high tide was at 10.17
vault.evidence: Tomorrow was the day, and it was some place where high tide was at 10:17.”
vault.hint: Think about the time in Scudder’s note.

vault.q: What was the house with the steps called?
vault.evidence: The house was called Trafalgar Lodge, and belonged to an old gentleman called Appleton—a retired stockbroker, the house-agent said.
vault.hint: Think about the villa on the cliff.

vault.q: What were the enemy spies called?
vault.evidence: You had better lie low, for if one of your Black Stone friends saw you there might be trouble.”
vault.hint: Think about the name Scudder’s notebook used.

vault.q: How did Hannay first escape from his flat?
vault.evidence: Lend me your cap and overall for ten minutes, and here’s a sovereign for you.”

vault.q: Who did Hannay pretend to be on the moor road?
vault.evidence: Then in a tiny bight of road, beside a heap of stones, I found the roadman.
